meta.title: Nguyên Tố — Interactive Periodic Table
meta.description: Interactive periodic table: electron configurations, atomic models, data and properties of all 118 elements.
meta.elementDescription: {nameEn}, atomic number {z}, atomic mass {mass}. Electron configuration {config}.

table.label: Periodic table of the chemical elements
table.hint: Hover to preview, click to open. Use arrow keys to move.
table.seriesLabel: {name} (atomic numbers {range}): shown in the row below

element.positionText: Period {period} because it has {period} electron shells; {block}-block because its last electron enters a {block} subshell.
element.predicted: Superheavy element: the electron configuration is a theoretical prediction.
element.exception: Exception to the Aufbau filling order.

photo.none: Nobody has ever made enough of this element to photograph it.

credits.title: Credits
credits.intro: Element photos are used under their authors' open licenses. Click an author to see the original.
credits.author: Author

academic.title: Chemistry corner
academic.hint: Electron configuration, atomic model, orbital diagram, data table, position in the table

radioactive.head: Every {name} atom will eventually decay
radioactive.sub: It has no stable form: this is a radioactive element

meltsInHand.head: It melts in the palm of your hand

density.perLitre: A 1-litre bottle full of it would weigh {kg} kg
density.perLitreGas: One litre of the gas weighs {g} g

melting.near: Melts at about the temperature of {landmark}

boiling.below: Only turns liquid when colder than {landmark}
boiling.near: Boils at about the temperature of {landmark}

landmark.coldestEarth: the coldest place ever measured on Earth (−89 °C)

atomsPerMm.head: You would need {count} atoms in a row to make 1 mm
atomsPerMm.sub: Each atom has a radius of about {r} pm (trillionths of a metre)

atomsPerGram.head: 1 gram holds about {count} atoms
atomsPerGram.headHypothetical: If you could collect 1 gram, it would hold about {count} atoms
atomsPerGram.subHypothetical: Nobody has ever made enough to weigh

body.name: In your body
body.desc: Just four elements, O, C, H and N, make up about 96% of your body mass. Tiles show the mass percentage, or grams in a 70 kg person for trace elements.

phone.name: In your phone
phone.desc: EuChemS counts 30 elements in a smartphone. These are the 20 whose supply is a concern. Red: serious threat within 100 years; orange: rising threat from increasing use; yellow: limited availability.

kitchen.name: In the kitchen
kitchen.desc: Elements you meet right in your kitchen: table salt, iodised salt, cast-iron pans, stainless steel pots, foil and tin cans. Sources are on each element's page.

precious.name: Precious
precious.desc: Precious metals: gold, silver and the six platinum-group metals. Rare, durable and almost never rust.

radioactive.name: Radioactive
radioactive.desc: 37 elements have no stable form: every one of their atoms will eventually decay.

liquid.name: Liquid (or almost)
liquid.desc: Mercury and bromine are liquid at room temperature. Gallium, caesium, rubidium and francium melt just a little warmer, below 40 °C.

synthetic.name: Lab-made only
synthetic.desc: The 24 elements from americium (95) onwards do not exist in nature; people make them, usually just a few atoms at a time.

safety.title: Safety
safety.radioactiveNote: Gives off harmful radiation. Only kept and handled in specialised laboratories.

colorMode.label: Colour by
colorMode.blockHint: The block tells you which subshell (s, p, d or f) the last electron goes into.
colorMode.wideHint: Put the lanthanides and actinides in their own rows
colorMode.compareHint: Tip: Shift + click a tile to add it to the comparison tray.

compare.title: Compare elements
compare.intro: Put up to 3 elements side by side. Each chart axis is one property, scaled from the lowest to the highest value in the whole periodic table.
compare.addHint: Add to the comparison tray (up to {max})
compare.empty: No elements selected yet. Type a name to add one.
compare.scaleNote: The centre is the lowest and the outer ring the highest value among all 118 elements; density uses a log scale. A hollow point at the centre means no data.

palette.title: Quick search
palette.placeholder: Type a name, symbol, number or use…

atom.builder: Build the atom electron by electron
atom.start: Press ▶ to fill the {count} electrons of {name} one by one.

rule.aufbau: Electron {index} goes into {sub}: the empty subshell with the lowest energy (Aufbau principle).
rule.hund: Electron {index} takes the next empty box in {sub}, with the same spin as the others (Hund's rule).
rule.pauli: Electron {index} pairs up, with opposite spin, in a box of {sub} (Pauli principle: at most 2 opposite-spin electrons per box).
rule.exception: Exception: measured experimentally, {symbol} has the configuration {config}. The subshell energies here are so close that the filling order no longer holds exactly.
rule.halfFull: A half-filled or full d subshell is more stable, so one electron moves from s to d.

atom.madelungLabel: Electron filling order diagram following the Madelung rule (increasing n + l)

ion.title: Ions
ion.cationRule: Positive ion: the atom loses {count, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}}, taken from the outermost shell (highest n) first. That is why transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d, even though 4s fills first.
ion.anionRule: Negative ion: the atom gains {count, plural, one {# electron} other {# electrons}}, which go into the next empty subshell in filling order.
ion.none: This element has no oxidation states in the data.

orbital.title: Orbital shapes
orbital.noWebgl: Your browser does not support WebGL: showing a 2D projection.
orbital.note: Each dot is a place the electron might be found; dense where it is likely. Shapes follow the hydrogen-atom solution; sizes are only qualitative. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.
